canonical_statement: The meta-analysis aimed to evaluate SGLT2 inhibitors for all-cause mortality, heart-failure hospitalization, NT-proBNP, left-ventricular systolic function, and diuretic efficiency in heart-failure patients regardless of ejection fraction or diabetes status.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: Objective: This study aims to evaluate the impact of SGLT2 inhibitors on all-cause mortality, heart failure hospitalization, and secondary outcomes...

canonical_statement: The authors reported conducting the review and meta-analysis according to PRISMA 2020.

source_anchor.verbatim_excerpt: A systematic review and a meta-analysis were conducted according to PRISMA 2020 guidelines.

canonical_statement: The literature search covered PubMed, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, Scopus, and Web of Science for randomized controlled trials published from January 2017 through November 2025.
Two reviewers conducted literature screening and selection, with a third senior reviewer resolving disagreements.
Eligible studies were prospective randomized controlled trials of SGLT2 inhibitors in adults with established heart failure, including HFrEF and HFpEF.
Eligible studies had to report at least one of all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, heart-failure hospitalization, NT-proBNP, left-ventricular systolic function, or diuretic effectiveness.

population.label: Eligible heart-failure trial population
inclusion_criteria: At least one prespecified clinical or functional outcome

canonical_statement: Both diabetic and non-diabetic participants were eligible if SGLT2-inhibitor use was for management of heart failure.

population.label: Heart-failure participants with or without diabetes
inclusion_criteria: SGLT2 inhibitor used for heart-failure management

canonical_statement: Trials with SGLT2 inhibitors as background therapy were eligible when heart-failure outcomes were prospectively evaluated, extractable, and stratified by treatment exposure.

population.label: Heart-failure trials with background SGLT2 inhibitor exposure

canonical_statement: The authors excluded non-randomized, observational, retrospective, registry-based studies, studies without a comparator arm, reviews, meta-analyses, case reports, editorials, and animal or in-vitro studies.
Only peer-reviewed records published from 2017 through 2025 were eligible.

Post-myocardial-infarction studies were eligible only when participants had established heart failure or documented left-ventricular dysfunction at baseline; prevention-only post-MI cohorts without heart failure were excluded.

population.label: Post-MI trial participants
inclusion_criteria: Established HF or documented LV dysfunction at baseline
exclusion_criteria: Prevention-only or high-risk post-MI cohort without HF

canonical_statement: Two reviewers independently extracted data with a piloted Microsoft Excel collection form and resolved disagreements by consensus.
For incomplete or unclear data, the authors reported that they would contact study authors and, if unresolved, estimate data from figures or supplementary material using digital extraction tools.
All-cause mortality was defined as death from any cause during trial follow-up.

outcome.definition: Death from any cause during trial follow-up

canonical_statement: Heart-failure hospitalization was defined as an emergency hospital admission for worsening heart failure with fluid-overload symptoms requiring intravenous diuretics or vasodilators.

outcome.definition: Emergency hospital admission for worsening HF with fluid overload requiring IV diuretics or vasodilators

canonical_statement: Secondary outcomes included NT-proBNP, left-ventricular systolic function, and diuretic function measured by urine volume, natriuresis, or loop-diuretic responsiveness.
The primary outcomes were pooled as hazard ratios with 95% confidence intervals; continuous outcomes were analyzed as mean differences or standardized mean differences.
Heterogeneity was quantified using I-squared, with 25%, 50%, and 75% described as low, moderate, and high heterogeneity; Cochran Q used p=0.10 as the significance cutoff.
The authors reported assessing both fixed-effect and random-effects models.
Publication bias was assessed by funnel plots, Egger regression, Begg and Mazumdar rank correlation, sensitivity analysis, and fail-safe N.
The database search identified 1,847 records.
After removal of 428 duplicates, 1,419 records were screened.
The PRISMA diagram reports 1,374 records excluded during screening, leaving 45 full-text articles assessed for eligibility.
The PRISMA diagram reports 30 full-text exclusions and 15 studies included in qualitative and quantitative synthesis.
The authors described the final synthesis as 15 randomized controlled trials with 28,484 participants.
The article reports included study sample sizes ranging from 23 to 6,263 participants.
The article reports participant mean ages from 59 to 73 years, male representation from 55% to 78%, and diabetes prevalence from 39% to 100% across studies.
The article states that all participants had a clinical diagnosis of heart failure at baseline.

The prose reports 10 trials at low risk of bias, four at moderate risk because of randomization or outcome-evaluation blinding, and one at moderate risk because of missing data and small sample size.

The authors described the mortality and hospitalization funnel plots as almost symmetric and concluded that small-study and selective-reporting bias were not an issue.
The authors interpreted the pooled estimates as a 14% reduction in all-cause mortality and a 26% reduction in heart-failure hospitalization with SGLT2 inhibitors.

The authors concluded that benefits were consistent across heart-failure phenotypes and diabetes status and described SGLT2 inhibitors as a cornerstone therapy for comprehensive heart-failure management.
The authors acknowledged heterogeneity in secondary endpoints related to participant differences, baseline treatment, and study duration.
The authors acknowledged that small mechanistic studies introduced variability despite sensitivity analyses.
The authors acknowledged limited participant-level granularity, including insufficient data for analyses by sex and renal function.
The authors stated that interactions with other guideline-directed therapies, treatment sequence, initiation timing, and acute heart failure require further study.
